newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Government said stable in Lesotho despite split.
newsitem.headline: Government said stable in Lesotho despite split.

text.p: Lesotho Prime Minister Ntsu Mokhehle's brother said on Friday a bitter rift in the ruling party would not weaken the government nor jeopardise a general poll next year.
Shakhane Mokhehle, minister of natural resources in his brother's government, told Reuters in an interview support for the premier remained strong despite his age and frailty.

In a dismissal of deputy Basotholand Congress Party leader Malopho Qhobela, he added: "There is a lot of support for the government and Qhobela's faction poses no challenge at all -- They are not weakening the government because they don't have a big following."

Diplomats say Ntsu Mokhehle, elected in 1993 as the first democratic leader in two decades, retains support from voters and party members. But constant wrangling between opposing factions in the ruling BCP and ineffective leadership by the 78-year-old premier has left a negative impression.
"Things are in such a mess," one diplomatic source, who declined to be named, told Reuters. "At a national, regional and international level the image of Lesotho is right down."

Prime Minister Mokhehle is currently fighting in court to overturn a resolution passed by Qhobela's faction in the BCP to dismiss him as party leader. However he announced last weekend he would not seek re-election in the March 1998 poll.
"He has had enough and he has said it is time that he makes room for younger people," Shakhane Mokhehle said.
The announcement was greeted with furrowed brows among the diplomatic community, with some sources saying it indicated a lack of effective leadership when it was most needed.
"The announcement has negatively affected the credibility of the government," one diplomat added.
The BCP split is between a minority of educated, urban voters for Qhobela's faction and larger rural support for Mokhehle, according to Khabela Matlosa, political scientist at the Lesotho University.
"The conflict between the two factions runs so deep now that they are unable to negotiate a settlement. It is now a question of winner takes all," Matlosa told Reuters.
The ailing Mokhehle has increasingly been absent from cabinet meetings and has left running the country to Deputy Prime Minister Pakalitha Mosisili.
Matlosa sees no easy victor in the leadership tussle.

"There is no real support for these politicians," he said. "Mokhehle's brother is not popular, Mosisili has no standing and is unable to rally any support from the people and Qhobela's faction appeals to mainly urban intellectual Basothos."
Ntsu Mokhehle has weathered a series of crises since he won power in March 1993. Last month an 11-day police munity was crushed by the army.
